item.research_question: Can high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in eutectic high entropy alloys (EHEAs) that are typically strong yet brittle?
item.material_system: Al0.7CoCrFeNi (Al 14.8 Co 21.3 Cr 21.3 Fe 21.3 Ni 21.3 at. %)
item.processing_route: Homogenized alloy subjected to HPHT treatment at 6 GPa and 1473 K for 2 hours using a self-designed hexahedron-anvil-press apparatus
item.test_conditions: Uniaxial quasi-static tensile tests at room temperature with a strain rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹
key_findings: The HPHT-treated alloy achieved a tensile strength of 1150 MPa and a tensile ductility of 36%, representing a doubling of both properties compared to the precursor.
The HPHT-treated alloy exhibited a true fracture stress of ~1570 MPa, significantly higher than the as-cast, as-cast+HPHT, and homogenized alloys.
The HPHT-treated alloy showed a uniform tensile elongation of ~36%, whereas the homogenized (Ho) alloy only exhibited ~14.7%.
The HPHT treatment induced a hierarchically patterned microstructure with hexagonal-like structural units interconnected by the FCC phase.
The mismatch factor between the FCC and B2 phases in the HPHT-treated alloy was calculated to be merely 0.004, indicating high coherency.
The HPHT-treated alloy displayed a homogeneous distribution of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) in both phases at 35% strain, unlike the Ho alloy.
Multiple deformation mechanisms including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands, and deformation twins were activated simultaneously in the HPHT-treated alloy.
item.mechanism: The HPHT-induced hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent FCC/B2 interfaces allows dislocations to transfer between phases, relieving stress concentration and preventing interfacial cracking. This coherency facilitates the progressive activation of multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocations, stacking faults, microbands, and twins) at multiple length scales, leading to strain delocalization and enhanced work hardening.
item.limitations: The text notes that predicting mechanical behaviors remains difficult due to the vast space of control parameters and complex microstructural evolution under extreme pressures, though it does not explicitly list limitations of the current study other than the need for further tuning of pressure and temperature.
item.future_work: The authors propose that the HPHT strategy can be generally applied to other alloy systems and pure metals (e.g., copper) to design advanced structural materials, and suggest that properties can be tuned by changing applied pressures and temperatures.
quotes: We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment.
Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms.
